prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

I Immense, august, like some Titanic bloom, The mighty choir unfolds its lithic core, Petalled with panes of azure, gules and or, Splendidly lambent in the Gothic gloom, And stamened with keen flamelets that illume The pale high-altar. On the prayer-worn floor, By worshippers innumerous thronged of yore, A few brown crones, familiars of the tomb, The stranded driftwood of Faith’s ebbing sea— For these alone the finials fret the skies, The topmost bosses shake their blossoms free, While from the triple portals, with grave eyes, Tranquil, and fixed upon eternity, The cloud of witnesses still testifies. II The crimson panes like blood-drops stigmatise The western floor. The aisles are mute and cold. A rigid fetich in her robe of gold, The Virgin of the Pillar, with blank eyes, Enthroned beneath her votive canopies, Gathers a meagre remnant to her fold. The rest is solitude; the church, grown old, Stands stark and grey beneath the burning skies. Well-nigh again its mighty framework grows To be a part of nature’s self, withdrawn From hot humanity’s impatient woes; The floor is ridged like some rude mountain lawn, And in the east one giant window shows The roseate coldness of an Alp at dawn.

outputs.L1:
I

Immense, august, like some Titanic bloom,  
The mighty choir unfolds its lithic core,  
Petalled with panes of azure, gules, and or,  
Splendidly lambent in the Gothic gloom,  
And stamened with keen flamelets that illume  
The pale high altar. On the prayer-worn floor,  
By worshippers innumerous thronged of yore,  
A few brown crones, familiars of the tomb,  
The stranded driftwood of Faith’s ebbing sea—  
For these alone the finials fret the skies,  
The topmost bosses shake their blossoms free,  
While from the triple portals, with grave eyes,  
Tranquil and fixed upon eternity,  
The cloud of witnesses still testifies.

II

The crimson panes, like blood-drops, stigmatise  
The western floor. The aisles are mute and cold.  
A rigid fetich in her robe of gold,  
The Virgin of the Pillar, with blank eyes,  
Enthroned beneath her votive canopies,  
Gathers a meagre remnant to her fold.  
The rest is solitude; the church, grown old,  
Stands stark and grey beneath the burning skies.  
Well-nigh again, its mighty framework grows  
To be a part of nature’s self, withdrawn  
From hot humanity’s impatient woes;  
The floor is ridged like some rude mountain lawn,  
And in the east one giant window shows  
The roseate coldness of an Alp at dawn.
outputs.L2:
I

Vast and solemn, resembling an enormous mythical flower, the great cathedral choir opens out its stone-built heart. Its petals are stained-glass panels of blue, red, and gold, glowing magnificently in the dim Gothic interior. Slender points of bright flame shine like stamens, casting light upon the pale high altar. On the floor, worn smooth by generations of prayer and once crowded with countless worshippers, only a few old brown-clad women remain, intimate with death—like pieces of driftwood left behind by the retreating tide of faith. For these few alone the spires still lace the sky, and the highest carved bosses seem to release their stone flowers. Meanwhile, above the three doorways, solemn-eyed, calm, and gazing toward eternity, the host of carved witnesses continues to bear silent testimony.

II

The red stained-glass windows stain the western pavement like fallen drops of blood. The aisles are silent and chill. The Virgin of the Pillar, stiff as an idol in her golden garment, sits beneath her offerings and canopies with empty, expressionless eyes, drawing only a thin remainder of believers around her. Beyond them there is only loneliness; the aged church stands bare and grey beneath the blazing sky. Its huge structure seems almost to be merging back into the natural world, removed from the restless sufferings of overheated human life. The floor rises and falls like a rough mountain meadow, and in the eastern wall a single enormous window reveals the rosy, icy pallor of an Alpine peak at daybreak.
outputs.L3:
The poem presents a grand Gothic cathedral as both immense and strangely organic, almost flower-like in its form and atmosphere. Its vast interior is dim, but it is not lifeless: stained-glass windows and candlelight fill the space with a subdued, glowing beauty. The building seems to bloom in shadow, its architectural details suggesting petals, stems, and intricate natural forms transformed into stone. This image gives the cathedral a sense of sacred grandeur, as though it is not merely a human construction but something living, rooted, and radiant.

At the same time, the poem stresses the contrast between the cathedral’s former purpose and its present emptiness. Once, it would have been crowded with worshippers, filled with voices, prayers, rituals, and communal faith. Now, however, only a few elderly women remain in attendance. Their presence suggests not vitality but survival: they are the last faithful remnants of a religious world that has largely passed away. Through this image, the poem evokes the decline of faith and the fading of collective devotion in the modern age.

Yet the cathedral itself continues to bear witness. Its statues, portals, finials, and carved figures remain fixed in place, solemn and enduring. These architectural and sculptural details seem like silent witnesses to eternity, preserving the beliefs and aspirations of those who built them. Even though human worshippers have largely disappeared, the stone forms continue their testimony. They stand as reminders of a spiritual vision that once shaped an entire culture, offering a sense of permanence in contrast to human forgetfulness and absence.

In the second section, the mood becomes even colder and more solitary. The church is presented as a place of stillness and abandonment, where the emptiness of the interior is emphasized by the chill atmosphere. Crimson light from the stained glass falls across the floor, creating a dramatic but lonely beauty. Before the Virgin, only a small remnant of worshippers gathers. This reduced congregation reinforces the sense that faith has diminished to a fragile survival, maintained by a few rather than shared by many.

Finally, the aging cathedral is imagined as returning to nature. Its stone structure is compared to mountains, suggesting that the building is gradually becoming part of the natural world rather than remaining a purely human monument. The great eastern window evokes an Alpine dawn, filling the image with grandeur and distance. In this vision, the cathedral seems to pass beyond history and religious practice into something elemental. Though human faith may decline, the cathedral endures as a vast, weathered presence, merging architecture, nature, and eternity.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents a meditation on the decline of religious devotion by setting the visible grandeur of a Gothic church against the diminished life within it. The building is described as a magnificent achievement of sacred architecture: its arches, stonework, height, and decorative richness still testify to the intensity of the faith that created it. Everything about the church’s design suggests aspiration, reverence, and communal worship. It was built to lift the mind beyond ordinary life, to turn human attention toward God, and to embody a belief system that once shaped society deeply.

Yet this architectural splendor is contrasted with an atmosphere of emptiness and fading use. The congregation is sparse, old, and dwindling, suggesting that the religious energy which once filled the church has largely disappeared. Instead of voices raised in collective prayer or song, the interior is marked by silence. The church remains physically impressive, but spiritually it seems almost abandoned. This contrast creates a sense of melancholy: the structure still possesses beauty and dignity, but it no longer functions as the living center of a vibrant faith community.

As the poem develops, the church begins to seem less like an active house of worship and more like an ancient object absorbed into the surrounding world. Its stones appear weathered by time; its presence becomes almost natural, like a cliff, hill, or grove. In this way, the poem suggests that the building has outlasted the beliefs and practices that brought it into being. Human devotion has ebbed, but the monument remains, changed in meaning by time. It is no longer only a symbol of religious certainty; it has become a relic, an aesthetic and historical presence, part of the landscape of memory.

The poem therefore reflects on the endurance of sacred art after the decline of the faith that inspired it. The church may no longer command the same devotion, but it still possesses power. Its beauty continues to move observers, even if they no longer share the beliefs of those who built it. In this sense, the poem does not simply mourn the loss of religion; it also recognizes that art can preserve traces of vanished conviction. The Gothic church stands as a reminder of what human beings once believed, created, and hoped for. Though faith has weakened, the form it took in stone endures, carrying forward a sacred atmosphere even in an age of silence and doubt.
outputs.L5:

Yet the story of the Titanic reminds us that even the most immense creations are not beyond the forces of nature. The tragedy became one of the most unforgettable events in history, teaching the world lessons about pride, safety, and the fragile line between confidence and disaster.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a two-part Petrarchan sonnet sequence in the style of a late Victorian poet describing a vast Gothic cathedral, using ornate imagery of stained glass, fading faith, old worshippers, and religious statuary.
counterfactuals.output:
**I. The Nave**

Beneath the vast and thunder-shadowed stone,  
Where saints in jewelled casements burn and bleed,  
The western light, like some expiring creed,  
Falls dim on aisles that age hath made its own.  
High up, the carven angels, cold and lone,  
Lean out with lips too marble-pure to plead,  
While censers of dead centuries seem to feed  
A ghostly fire about the altar-throne.  

Here bowed the old, with hands like winter leaves,  
Their murmured aves faltering into air;  
And some, whose eyes no earthly dawn receives,  
Still turn blind faces toward the painted prayer.  
But through the dusk a waning splendour grieves:  
Faith’s rose is sweet, though death be at its core.  

**II. The Chapels**

In chapels drowned with violet and gold,  
The Virgin smiles, remote from grief and time;  
A martyr lifts, amid the dust sublime,  
His stone-bound palm, forever young, yet old.  
The windows blaze with kings and prophets scrolled  
In crimson legend, azure dream, and rime;  
Yet underneath, the bells’ remembered chime  
Sleeps faint as incense in a thurible cold.  

O house of God, where God seems far away,  
Thy pillars climb like prayers that lose their breath;  
Thy saints stand patient in the ashen ray,  
Half crowned with glory and half crowned with death.  
Still, when the last pale worshippers shall stray,  
Thou wilt keep watch with Beauty for their faith.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an original poem with sections I and II about an ancient cathedral in decline, full of Gothic architectural details, melancholy religious symbolism, and comparisons to nature, in elevated archaic language.
counterfactuals.output:
**I**

Behold, where once the minster lifted high  
Her thornéd spires into the trembling blue,  
She leaneth now beneath a wolf-gray sky,  
With all her saints worn faceless by the dew.  
The gargoyles, crouched like ravens carved in grief,  
Spout ancient tears from throats of blackened stone;  
And round each arch, as round an autumn leaf,  
The patient moss hath made a crownless throne.

Her windows, jewel-bruised with saints and kings,  
Are cracked like ice on some forsaken mere;  
Through them the evening’s pallid angel flings  
A blood-red beam, and vanisheth in fear.  
The nave, once loud with censers and with psalms,  
Now hears but rain, and wind in cassocks torn;  
The clustered columns rise like winter palms,  
Bare, spectral, to a roof by thunder shorn.

There lies the altar, dim with dust and time,  
Where candles guttered as frail souls in prayer;  
The cross above, made green with cankered rime,  
Hangs like a dead bough in the bitter air.  
O house of God, what slow eclipse is thine—  
What lichen-script upon thy ribs is spread!  
The ivy creepeth, like a darkened vine,  
To bind the living stones among the dead.

**II**

At midnight, when the moon with silver nail  
Fasteneth clouds upon the firmament,  
The cathedral sighs beneath her tattered veil,  
A widow’d queen in holy ruin bent.  
Her flying buttresses, those stony wings,  
No longer yearn as swallows toward the sun;  
They brood like cliffs where no sweet creature sings,  
And take the rain as penance, one by one.

The choir-stalls, gnawed by worm and prayer alike,  
Keep still the impress of the vanished knees;  
There silence sits, with finger thin and white,  
And counts the beads of dropping eaves.  
No bell now rolleth from the tower’s height  
To wake the graves that cluster at her side;  
Only the owl, that monk of eyeless night,  
Repeats his hollow office far and wide.

Yet in her wounds some solemn beauty stays:  
As forests wear the splendor of decay,  
So doth she gather, through her failing days,  
A darker grace no dawn may quite betray.  
For God, perchance, in broken arches dwells,  
And bends more near where shattered roses fall;  
While roots, like psalms from subterranean cells,  
Climb upward, praying, through the crumbled wall.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a pair of 14-line sonnets that evoke the atmosphere of a nearly empty medieval church, with stained-glass colors, a high altar, crones at prayer, the Virgin Mary, and a sense of Christianity ebbing away.
counterfactuals.output:
**I**

In nave-cold dusk the stained glass spills its wine,  
Blue saints dissolve in pools of ruby flame;  
A green-gold angel, cracked along the spine,  
Still lifts a trumpet no one comes to claim.  
The high altar gathers dust and beeswax tears,  
Its linen yellowed, silver dulled with air;  
Three crones kneel muttering their childhood fears,  
Their beads like bones passed hand to hand in prayer.  
Above them, Mary, mild in painted grief,  
Bends down her face through centuries of smoke;  
Her starry mantle, fading leaf by leaf,  
Shelters a faith grown thin as candle smoke.  
Outside, the rooks wheel black against the day;  
Inside, the old God softly ebbs away.  

**II**

The choir stalls gape, their carven demons worn  
Smooth by the sleeves of choristers long dead;  
A bell-rope hangs, but no one rings the morn,  
And moss creeps near the threshold, green as bread.  
The windows bruise the flagstones violet, red,  
As if old martyrs bled there, drop by drop;  
The altar waits, with no young server led  
To light the wicks or make the censers hop.  
Only the crones remain, bent-backed and small,  
Whispering Hail Marys into the stone;  
The Virgin listens from her painted wall,  
Her infant dim, her lilies overgrown.  
The last Amen drifts upward, frail and gray,  
While Christendom goes quietly away.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: I want a decadent 19th-century-style poem about a grand Gothic basilica as if it were a stone flower, contrasting its former crowds of worshippers with present solitude under hot skies.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Basilica in the Heat**

Behold the church, a monstrous flower of stone,  
Black-lilied, rooted in the old dead square,  
Whose petals are the buttresses upthrown,  
Whose thorns are saints that menace from the air;  
A blossom carved by centuries of prayer,  
It opens, cold, beneath the brazen noon,  
And drinks the sun with windows dim and rare,  
Like veins of blood in some funereal bloom.

Once, through its doors, as through a chaliced bell,  
The multitudes in tidal darkness rolled;  
The poor, the proud, the plague-struck, and the well,  
The wives in linen, knights in spurs of gold.  
Their breath made clouds; their murmurs, manifold,  
Rose like a hive about the altar’s flame,  
While censers swung their little moons of cold,  
And every mouth was burning with one Name.

Then music, vast as purple thunder, poured  
From organ-pipes like caverns full of storm;  
The lifted Host flashed like a little sword,  
And kneeling bodies made the pavement warm.  
Faith, that pale empress in her awful form,  
Moved robed in incense down the shadowed nave;  
And every capital, grotesque and worn,  
Leered over hope, and leaned above the grave.

But now—how still the great corolla stands!  
No pilgrim presses where the lichens creep;  
No ringed episcopal, indulgent hands  
Scatter the stars of blessing on the sheep.  
The chapels hold their ornamental sleep;  
A spider threads the Virgin’s silver crown;  
In crypts of air the drowsy echoes keep  
The Latin dust of an abandoned town.

The sun, a tyrant with a golden lash,  
Strikes on the towers till the gargoyles glare;  
The pavements split; the painted windows flash  
Their saints in fevered rubies on the air.  
Hot skies, immense, unpitying, and bare,  
Lean close above the flower’s blackened crest,  
As if to scorch the last cool bud of prayer  
That once lay folded in its marble breast.

O stone camellia of a vanished God,  
Magnificent, diseased, and desolate,  
Still do you bloom from consecrated sod,  
Too proud for ruin and too sad for fate.  
The swallows pass your arches; shadows wait  
Like widowed queens along the aisles of bone;  
And in your heart, grown splendidly ornate,  
Solitude kneels where thousands knelt—alone.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a formal, rhymed poem in two numbered parts, using rich vocabulary and imagery, about a cathedral whose windows, finials, portals, and statues still testify to faith despite abandonment.
counterfactuals.output:
I.

Beneath the rooks’ slow wheeling over stone,  
The cathedral lifts its weather-darkened face;  
Though grass has claimed the nave, and winds intone  
Their vespers through the aisles of vacant space,  
The windows, bruised with ruby, gold, and blue,  
Still kindle saints in panes of shattered fire;  
Their fractured glories sift the morning through  
Like psalms remembered by a ruined choir.  

The portals, deep with vines and lichened script,  
Hold angels in their archivolts of shade;  
Each threshold, by neglect and tempest stripped,  
Still seems for pilgrim-knees and mercy made.  
No bell replies, no priestly footfalls pass—  
Yet heaven burns in every shard of glass.  

II.

The finials, thinned by centuries of rain,  
Still prick the clouds with supplicating spears;  
They sign the sky with an ascetic pain,  
Sharp as a prayer preserved beyond its years.  
And statues, robbed of fingers, crowns, and names,  
Keep vigil in their mutilated grace;  
Their hollow eyes, unlit by altar-flames,  
Look past the dusk toward an eternal place.  

Though ivy clasps the transept like a pall,  
Though foxgloves root where censers once were swung,  
Faith has not fled the fractured, sacred wall,  
Nor left the stones without a chanted tongue.  
Abandoned, still it stands—severe, sublime—  
A creed in limestone, preaching down through time.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
